chunks: As for what Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥasan al-Ṣaffār narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Munabbih, from al-Ḥusayn ibn ʿUlwān, from ʿAmr ibn Khālid, from Zayd ibn ʿAlī, from his forefathers, from ʿAlī عليه السلام, who said:

I sat performing wudu (ablution), and the Messenger of Allah صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم came as I had begun the wudu (ablution). He said to me: “Rinse your mouth, draw water into the nose, and clean the teeth.” Then I washed my face three times, so he said: “Two times of that may suffice you.” He said: “Then I washed my forearms and wiped my head twice, so he said: ‘One time of that may suffice you.’ And I washed my feet.” Then he said to me: “O ʿAlī, pass between the toes; do not let them be interlaced by the Fire.”

So this report agrees with the position of the generality and has come in the context of taqiyyah, because what is known from the doctrine of the Imams عليهم السلام is wiping the feet in wudu (ablution), not washing them. That is more well-known than that doubt should occur to anyone concerning it. If the matter is as we have stated, then it is not permissible for the reports we have presented, nor the apparent meaning of the Qur’an, to be opposed by it.

Then he said, may Allah Exalted support him: If one forgets to clean his feet by washing before the wudu (ablution), or delays it for some reason among reasons, then he should place an interval between that and his wudu (ablution), and separate the two by a period of time, whether short or long, and he should not join them together, so that he may distinguish the wudu (ablution) that is commanded from something else. Its explanation, and what is of its meaning, has already passed.

Then he said, may Allah Exalted support him: There is no sunnah (prophetic tradition) nor merit in wiping the ears, and whoever wipes the outside of his ears and their inside has introduced an innovation. What indicates this is that washing the limbs in taharah (ritual purity) and wiping them is a legal ruling, so one should follow in that a legal proof. There is nothing in the sacred law that indicates the obligation of wiping the ears in wudu (ablution), and whoever establishes in the sacred law a ruling without a legal proof is an innovator, without disagreement among the Muslims. This too is indicated by further evidence.

key_terms.التَّقِيَّةِ: dissimulation under circumstances requiring precaution, used here to explain the report’s context
key_terms.الطَّهَارَةِ: ritual purity and its legal procedures
key_terms.الْوُضُوءِ: wudu (ablution), the ritual purification before acts of worship
key_terms.سُنَّةٌ: a legislated prophetic tradition or recommended practice
key_terms.غَسْلِهِمَا: washing them, i.e., the feet, contrasted with wiping
key_terms.فَضِيلَةٌ: special merit or virtue in devotional practice
key_terms.مَسْحُ الرِّجْلَيْنِ: wiping the feet, identified here as the established Imamī ruling in wudu (ablution)
key_terms.مُبْدِعٌ: one who introduces an innovation into the religion without legal proof

ai.seo_question: What does Tahdhīb al-Aḥkām say about wiping or washing the feet and ears in wudu (ablution)?
ai.summary: This passage discusses rulings of wudu (ablution), including a report about the Prophet صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم instructing Imam ʿAlī عليه السلام during ablution, followed by a juristic clarification on how the report is understood. It emphasizes, in line with Imamī teaching, wiping the feet rather than washing them, the need to distinguish ordinary washing from wudu (ablution), and that wiping the ears is not part of the legislated practice.
